concept.name: Tape reading
concept.definition: The practice of inferring short-term buying and selling pressure by watching the stream of executed trades — originally the ticker tape, today the time-and-sales window — focusing on trade size, speed, and whether prints occur at the bid or the ask. It is one of the oldest forms of order-flow analysis, descending from the era of Wyckoff and Livermore.
concept.intuition: Instead of studying charts after the fact, the tape reader watches each transaction as it happens, sensing urgency from the rhythm and size of the prints.
concept.mechanics: The trader monitors the T&S stream for accelerating print rates, repeated large prints at the offer or bid, stalling price on heavy prints (absorption), and uptick/downtick sequences, forming an intraday read that complements or replaces chart analysis.
concept.failure_modes: In modern fragmented, algorithmic markets the tape is dominated by HFT micro-prints and iceberg slicing, so the 'rhythm' that classical tape readers relied on is largely machine-generated noise; skill is extremely screen-time dependent.
concept.misconceptions: Tape reading is not a mystical art that reveals manipulation on demand; it is pattern recognition on execution data, and its classical literature predates electronic markets whose microstructure differs fundamentally.
concept.example: A scalper sees sell prints accelerating into 4,498 while price stops ticking down; reading possible absorption on the tape, they stand aside from new shorts until the level resolves.
